findings.title: Fsync fatal handling lost
findings.body:
`sync_all()` errors used to go through `.maybe_fatal_err("delta_layer sync_all")`, which aborts the process on fatal I/O errors. They are now wrapped in a plain recoverable `anyhow` error.

A failed fsync can leave the kernel's dirty pages dropped, and a later retry may report success on lost data. Compaction or flush could then retry and register a layer that is not durable, risking silent data loss.

The same regression is in `image_layer.rs` (`image_layer sync_all`). Keep `maybe_fatal_err` and map its result into the new error enum.

findings.title: Fsync fatal handling lost
findings.body: This is the same regression as in the delta layer: `.maybe_fatal_err("image_layer sync_all")` was replaced by a plain `anyhow` error. Fsync failures, including fatal ones like EIO, now become retryable errors instead of aborting the process, which can lead to non-durable image layers being considered valid.

findings.title: Cancellation type erased
findings.body:
The PR adds typed `Cancelled` variants, but every caller flattens them back into `anyhow::anyhow!("flush task cancelled")` wrapped in `CompactionError::Other` or `CreateImageLayersError::Other`. Some call sites go further and detect cancellation by matching on `e.to_string()`.

Previously the original `FlushTaskError` value stayed inside the anyhow chain, where it could be downcast. Now only a string remains, so any downstream cancellation detection (e.g. `root_cause().downcast_ref`) cannot recognise it. Shutdown-time cancellations may then be reported as real compaction or image-creation errors, with error logs and metrics.

The string-match branches are also no-ops: both arms produce `Other`. Map `Cancelled` to the callers' existing cancellation variants, or at least preserve a typed error.

Uncertain: whether downstream code currently relies on such a downcast.
